newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - No Euro without Germany and France - Duisenberg.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - No Euro without Germany and France - Duisenberg.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenburg said on Friday Europe's single currency project could not proceed without Germany and France on board and he assumed monetary union would start as planned in 1999.

Speaking to reporters before a conference on global economic convergence in the Dutch seaside resort of Noordwijk, Duisenberg said: "I don't think it would make much sense to have a common currency area without Germany and France."

Duisenberg is due to take over on July 1 as head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the European Central Bank (ECB), which is scheduled to run monetary policy under EMU from 1999. He is also widely regarded as a strong candidate to become the first president of the ECB.
Asked if he believed economic and monetary union (EMU) would start on time in January 1999, he told reporters: "I'm working on that (assumption)."
He rejected suggestions that the recent appointment of a Socialist-led government in France and Germany's budgetary problems could force a delay in the single currency project.

Duisenberg said he did not believe Germany's recent decision not to use the proceeds of a revaluation of gold reserves to improve its 1997 budget position would adversely affect its prospects of meeting the EMU entry criteria on time.
Adressing the conference, Duisenberg said he expected a "great majority" of the European Union's 15 member states to be particpating in EMU by 2000.
Five unspecified EU states already met the criteria for EMU entry and that the others were "on their way" to meet them.

"I think that by the year 2000 there will be a great majority of European Union member states participating in monetary union," he told the ABN AMRO conference on "Convergence of Three Economic World Powers".
Duisenberg told his audience they should not be impressed by one-off measures which countries might take to fulfil the EMU entry criteria: "It's the sustainability which is important."
Germany, France, Spain, Portugal and Italy had made great efforts to meet the entry requirements, he said.

The loss of the ability to adjust exchanges rates between European countries was sometimes seen as one of the main disadvantages of economic and monetary (EMU), the process which creates a single European currency, the euro.

"Nevertheless, I believe it is this very factor which underscores why strict interpretation of the convergence criteria contained in the Maastricht Treaty is essential to the viability of monetary union,"
He also said proponents of the view that the stability pact would lead to the relinquishment of budgetary policy as an instrument of stabilisation did not fully understand how the pact worked.
The pact aims to ensure that fiscal discipline will be maintained, after EMU begins, among member countries adopting the single European currency.
He said the pact boosted discipline by way of the explicit agreement that EMU member states must, on average, strive for a budget close to balance or in surplus.
Duisenberg also denied that the pact would sap budgetary policy of all flexibility, leaving only a rigid structure incapable of absorbing cyclical adversity.
"If, in times of boom, (EMU) member states record budget surpluses, they will be very well placed to cope adequately with cyclical adversity," he said.
"I am firmly convinced that if public finances are sound, the stability pact will prove flexible enough," he added.
